summary: This proposed standard captures the semantics of the Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement part of the CDNI Request Routing interface, meaning what Footprint and Capabilities should mean in the CDNI context and what the advertisement interface offers.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending orders to a partner, you need to know where it delivers and what it can do. This explains exactly what those two things mean.

subtitle: What 'footprint' and 'capabilities' mean when one CDN tells another where and how it can deliver content.

tldr.problem: When CDNs interconnect, an upstream CDN must know where a downstream CDN can serve users and which features it supports before handing it requests. 'Footprint' and 'capabilities' were loosely defined.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the meaning of both terms, chooses the model of 'capabilities with footprint restrictions', and defines a JSON base advertisement object plus five initial capability objects and an IANA registry of redirection modes.
tldr.outcome: It gives CDNI protocols a common vocabulary and a place to extend it, but it does not define a transport protocol for the advertisements. It has since been updated by RFC 9388.

today: RFC 8008 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9388. It defines the meaning and objects for footprint and capability advertisement but, by its own scope, leaves the transport protocol to other documents.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The CDNI working group is building protocols that let several content delivery networks (CDNs) interconnect, for example to extend one CDN's reach into areas it does not cover. This RFC is about the Footprint & Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI), part of CDNI Request Routing. Through it, a downstream CDN (dCDN) tells an upstream CDN (uCDN) about its footprint and capabilities.

The RFC states the problem plainly: the range of possible footprint definitions and capabilities is very broad, and trying to define a comprehensive solution quickly becomes intractable. So it only pins down the meaning of the terms and the semantics of the two advertisements. Choosing a concrete FCI protocol is explicitly out of scope, although the RFC gives guidelines for such protocols.

It assumes the CDNs have already bootstrapped and can exchange information, and that the uCDN receives the initial Request Routing message from the endpoint asking for the resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine several pizza chains teaming up. This RFC does not choose how they phone each other. It only agrees on what 'where we deliver' and 'what we can do' mean.

sections.title: Footprint and Capability Defined
sections.content:
A footprint is a description of a CDN's coverage area: the area from which client requests may originate and to which the CDN is willing to deliver content. It can be written as an address range (IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR), a network ID such as an ASN, a country code, or GPS coordinates. The RFC does not endorse any one method; it only defines how to transport known footprint descriptions.

A capability is a feature of a dCDN that the uCDN relies on when deciding to delegate a request. Support can change over time and can be limited to part of the dCDN's footprint. The RFC describes a scheme for defining new capabilities and carrying them, not a complete list.
sections.plainLanguage: A footprint is the map of streets you deliver to. A capability is something you can do there, like delivering in a box or in a bag.

sections.title: Design Decisions
sections.content:
Much of the difficulty is deciding what 'coverage' even means. A Surrogate with a public IPv4 address is reachable from any endpoint unless policy blocks it, so a limited footprint is usually an administrative choice. A global CDN would presumably cover all prefixes, while a purpose-built ISP CDN may cover only its own subscribers. The RFC points out that coverage need not be binary: a dCDN could advertise a coverage 'score', or the addresses of its Surrogates.

Capabilities can be static (total storage) or highly dynamic (storage in use). The RFC also weighs advertisements against queries: if a uCDN tracked detailed state for thousands of Surrogates, the volume of updates would not scale, and querying dCDNs per request (as in recursive redirection) might be better.

Finally, a dCDN might 'cheat' by advertising inaccurate information to win traffic. The RFC says advertised information should be verifiable in the long run, perhaps by out-of-band audits, and that strong contractual agreements add a deterrent.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling a partner exactly where you can deliver is harder than it sounds. Some things never change, some change every minute, and someone might fib to win more orders.

sections.title: Capabilities with Footprint Restrictions
sections.content:
From these trade-offs the FCI takes a simple stance. It assumes the uCDN makes the delegation decision from what it receives, that cheating is handled outside CDNI, and that advertised information is accurate. It leaves out qualitative information such as Surrogate proximity, delivery latency or load.

Because contracts usually define the basic coverage, the FCI mainly delivers updates to the basic capabilities and coverage. The chosen semantics are therefore capabilities with footprint restrictions. Appendix B adds that footprints act as constraints on delegation, and that multiple footprint constraints are additive: each type narrows the dCDN's candidacy further. Appendix C says highly dynamic capabilities, such as real-time delivery metrics or CDN load, are beyond the scope of the FCI.
sections.plainLanguage: The big deals are settled in a contract beforehand. This system is only for little updates, like 'we cannot deliver to this street today'.

sections.title: Extending Footprints and Capabilities
sections.content:
Other footprint types may be defined later, using the 'CDNI Metadata Footprint Types' registry from RFC 8006. This RFC registers CDNI Payload Types for five initial capability types: Delivery Protocol, Acquisition Protocol, Redirection Mode, CDNI Logging and CDNI Metadata. Each is prefixed with FCI.. An updated capability object MUST be given a newly registered Payload Type, for example by appending .v2.

Not every implementation supports every optional type, so any FCI protocol MUST define how support is negotiated and how failures or unsupported types are handled. A uCDN MAY ignore capability or footprint types it does not understand and decide on the ones it does.

For logging, CDNs SHOULD NOT advertise mandatory-to-implement record-types or fields; optional fields are advertised within a specific record-type. For metadata, advertising mandatory-to-enforce GenericMetadata types MUST be provided, and advertising other types SHOULD be provided.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of things you can announce is meant to grow. Any partner that does not know a new item can just skip it and use the ones it understands.

sections.title: The Advertisement Objects
sections.content:
The base object, FCIBase, has three properties. capability-type is a CDNI Payload Type and is mandatory to specify. capability-value holds the capability object, whose format depends on the type, and is also mandatory. footprints is an optional list of CDNI Footprint objects.

Objects MUST be encoded in JSON and MUST follow the I-JSON recommendations. Property names defined by this document MUST be lowercase.

The five capability objects are:

  • delivery-protocols: supported delivery protocols, taken from the 'CDNI Metadata Protocol Types' registry.
  • acquisition-protocols: supported protocols for acquiring content from the uCDN or origin.
  • redirection-modes: supported modes from the new redirection-mode registry.
  • record-type and optional fields for logging. Omitting fields means all optional fields are supported; an empty list means none.
  • metadata: supported GenericMetadata types. An empty list means only structural metadata and simple types are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Each announcement is a small labelled form: what kind of thing, what the answer is, and optionally which areas it applies to.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registers five Payload Types: FCI.DeliveryProtocol, FCI.AcquisitionProtocol, FCI.RedirectionMode, FCI.Logging and FCI.Metadata. It also creates the 'CDNI Capabilities Redirection Modes' registry, where additions follow the IETF Review policy.

The initial entries are DNS-I and DNS-R (iterative and recursive DNS-based redirection) and HTTP-I and HTTP-R (iterative and recursive HTTP-based redirection).
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book gets an official list of the five kinds of announcement and four ways of pointing a customer to the right helper.

sections.title: Security Requirements for FCI Protocols
sections.content:
This RFC defines semantics, not a transport, so it can only place constraints on protocols that carry them. All such protocols are REQUIRED to provide integrity and authentication. Without them, an attacker could forge an advertisement claiming a dCDN has no footprint or capability and so stop the uCDN from delegating to it.

They are also REQUIRED to provide confidentiality, because a dCDN may share information such as a temporary outage with the uCDN but not with competing dCDNs. The RFC says these needs could be met by transport-layer security with domain certificates, for example TLS for HTTP, and that no further object-level security seems necessary because trust is bilateral between a uCDN and a dCDN.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages between partners must be sealed and signed, so nobody can fake a note saying 'we cannot deliver' and nobody else can read your private news.
